chapters.title: Chapter 5: Risk Management for Trend and Momentum Strategies

lessons.title: Why Trend and Momentum Strategies Have Fat Tails and Long Drawdowns

children.text: Every strategy in this course so far has carried the same quiet warning attached: momentum crashes exist, whipsaws happen, backtests can flatter results. This chapter turns those warnings into an actual risk management framework, starting with the statistical shape of these strategies' returns, which is nothing like the tidy, symmetric bell curve most introductory finance material assumes.

body.text: Trend and momentum strategy returns are not normally distributed. They typically show fat tails, extreme outcomes more frequent than a normal distribution predicts, and for cross-sectional momentum specifically, negative skew, many small gains punctuated by occasional sharp, large losses. Simple average return and simple volatility, on their own, understate how much this shape actually matters.

children.text: What 'Fat Tails' and 'Negative Skew' Actually Mean

body.caption: Skewness measures asymmetry: negative skew means the distribution has a longer, heavier left tail, large losses are more extreme than large gains. Excess kurtosis measures tail thickness relative to a normal distribution: positive excess kurtosis means extreme outcomes, in either direction, happen more often than a bell curve would predict.

body.title: Illustrative monthly return distribution: normal vs momentum-like (illustrative frequencies)

body.text: Notice the momentum-like distribution has more months clustered in the small, steady 0-5% gain bucket than the normal distribution does, but also a noticeably fatter left tail below -10%. This combination, frequent small wins plus occasional severe losses, is the practical signature of negative skew, and it is exactly what makes these strategies feel deceptively smooth right up until they aren't.

children.text: Cross-Sectional Momentum's Crash Risk: A Recap

Chapter 1's case study already showed the mechanism: after a sharp market bottom, past losers, often high-beta names, rebound faster than past winners, hurting a long-short cross-sectional momentum portfolio's short leg badly during exactly the kind of sharp market recovery that should otherwise feel like good news. Daniel and Moskowitz's 2016 research found this pattern is systematic, not a one-off event specific to March 2020, which is why cross-sectional equity momentum specifically carries well-documented negative skew concentrated around sharp trend reversals.
Trend Following's Different Tail Profile: 'Crisis Alpha'

Time-series trend following, the subject of Chapter 2, behaves differently in a crisis, and it is worth being precise about why. Because a trend-following system can flip to short as a sustained decline develops, research by Hurst, Ooi, and Pedersen at AQR, in their widely cited 2013 paper 'Demystifying Managed Futures,' found that trend-following strategies have historically tended to post positive average returns during the market's largest, most sustained drawdowns, the dot-com bust and the 2008 global financial crisis among them, a pattern the paper calls crisis alpha. This is not a free lunch. Trend followers need time to actually flip short as a decline unfolds, so an extremely sudden, single-week crash, like the initial days of March 2020, can still hurt a trend-following book before its signals have time to react, and the strategy remains exposed to its own whipsaw losses in choppy, directionless markets, as Chapter 2 covered directly.

body.text: Do not read 'crisis alpha' as 'trend following cannot lose money in a crash.' It means trend following has historically had a more favorable average relationship with major sustained crises than cross-sectional momentum has, not that either strategy is immune to a sudden, sharp loss. Both are still capable of fat left tails, just from somewhat different sources.

children.text: Measuring the Real Risk: Beyond Simple Volatility

A strategy's simple volatility, or a Sharpe ratio built from it, treats a big upside month and a big downside month as equally significant contributors to risk, which is precisely wrong for a negatively skewed strategy. The Sortino ratio fixes this by only penalizing downside volatility, the deviation of returns below a minimum acceptable threshold, leaving upside swings, which no trader actually minds, out of the risk calculation entirely.

body.caption: The Sortino ratio: excess return over a minimum acceptable return (MAR), divided by downside deviation, which only measures volatility from returns that fall below that threshold.

children.text: Alongside Sortino, max drawdown, introduced in Chapter 2's backtesting case study, remains one of the most honest risk numbers for these strategies precisely because it captures the tail event directly rather than averaging it away into a single volatility figure.

body.title: One bad month, big impact
body.prompt: A momentum strategy has 9 months of +2% returns and 1 month of -10%. What is its average monthly return over these 10 months, in percent?
body.explanation: (9 x 2 + 1 x -10) / 10 = (18 - 10) / 10 = 0.8%. Despite winning 90% of the months, the single -10% month drags the average down to well under half of what a steady +2% a month would have produced, exactly the practical bite of negative skew and fat tails.

body.title: Crisis alpha vs crash risk
body.question: Which statement most accurately reflects the difference covered in this lesson between trend following and cross-sectional momentum during major market crises?
options: Both strategies are completely immune to losses during any crisis

Trend following has historically shown a tendency toward positive returns during major sustained crises, while cross-sectional momentum has well-documented crash risk concentrated around sharp market rebounds
Cross-sectional momentum always outperforms trend following during a crisis
Neither strategy's behavior during a crisis has ever been studied academically
body.explanation: Hurst, Ooi, and Pedersen documented trend following's historical 'crisis alpha' during sustained bear markets, while Daniel and Moskowitz documented cross-sectional momentum's crash risk specifically around sharp market rebounds. Neither finding means either strategy is risk-free.

body.title: Choosing the right risk metric
body.scenario: Two strategies have identical average annual return and identical standard deviation of returns, giving them identical Sharpe ratios. Strategy A's losing months are all small and similar in size. Strategy B has mostly small gains but two very large, sharp losing months.
body.prompt: Based on this lesson, why might the Sharpe ratio be misleading two investors comparing these strategies, and what would a Sortino ratio or max drawdown figure reveal instead?
body.modelAnswer: The Sharpe ratio treats all deviation from the average as equally risky, so it cannot distinguish between Strategy A's mild, evenly spread losses and Strategy B's two severe, concentrated losses, even though Strategy B is clearly riskier to actually hold through. A Sortino ratio would penalize Strategy B more heavily, since it only measures downside deviation and Strategy B's downside is far more extreme. Max drawdown would show the difference even more starkly, likely revealing a much deeper peak-to-trough decline for Strategy B despite the two strategies sharing the same headline Sharpe ratio.

body.description: AQR's public research library includes Hurst, Ooi, and Pedersen's original work on trend following's crisis alpha, worth reading in full before relying on this lesson's summary of it.

body.title: Fat Tails and Drawdowns: Core Terms

cards.definition: A return distribution property where extreme outcomes occur more frequently than a normal distribution would predict, measured by positive excess kurtosis.
A return distribution property where losses are more extreme than gains, typically many small wins punctuated by occasional large losses.
The historical tendency of trend-following strategies to post positive returns during major, sustained market crises, documented by Hurst, Ooi, and Pedersen.
A risk-adjusted return measure that penalizes only downside deviation below a minimum acceptable return, unlike the Sharpe ratio, which penalizes all volatility equally.

points: Trend and momentum strategy returns are typically not normally distributed, showing fat tails and, for cross-sectional momentum specifically, negative skew.
Cross-sectional momentum's crash risk clusters around sharp market rebounds, per Daniel and Moskowitz's research, already illustrated in Chapter 1's case study.

Trend following has historically shown a different pattern, 'crisis alpha,' positive average returns during major sustained crises, per Hurst, Ooi, and Pedersen, though it remains exposed to sudden shocks and its own whipsaw losses.
Simple volatility and the standard Sharpe ratio understate tail risk for negatively skewed strategies. The Sortino ratio and max drawdown are more honest measures.

None of this is abstract: a strategy can win 90% of the time and still have its average return gutted by a single severe month, exactly why position sizing and exit discipline, covered next, matter as much as the signal itself.
